where: Section 3 (also Exam trap 3, Q6 answer, figure caption)
problem: The claim that equal covariance matrices and equal priors make the Bayes boundary 'exactly the minimum distance boundary' is false for a general covariance matrix. Equal covariance Σ gives a linear Bayes boundary, but the rule is nearest mean under Mahalanobis distance (x−m_j)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−m_j). Only when Σ is a scalar multiple of the identity, Σ = σ²I, does that reduce to Euclidean nearest mean, with the boundary as the perpendicular bisector of m₁m₂. Q6 repeats the error ('With equal priors it is the minimum distance line') and so do the figure caption and Exam trap 3.
fix: Say: for Gaussian classes with equal, isotropic covariance σ²I and equal priors, the Bayes boundary is exactly the minimum distance boundary (the perpendicular bisector). With equal but general Σ the Bayes rule uses the Mahalanobis distance; the boundary is still a straight line but is not the perpendicular bisector. Correct Q6, the figure caption and Exam trap 3 the same way.

problem: 'Manhattan distance adds absolute coordinate differences' is loose; it is the sum of those differences, not an extra term added to Euclidean distance.
fix: Manhattan distance is the sum of the absolute coordinate differences, Σ|x_i − y_i|, and is an option.

problem: The four counts (true positive, false positive, true negative, false negative) describe a two-class problem; for J classes the confusion matrix is J×J and these counts are taken per class. A student may think a confusion matrix is always 2×2.
fix: For two classes a confusion matrix holds true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives; for J classes it is a J×J table, with these four counts read off one class at a time.

problem: HOG is called a small feature set, but a standard HOG descriptor for one detection window has thousands of components, so the example misleads about when these classifiers are cheap.
fix: Say 'small or medium feature sets such as colour histograms or short HOG summaries'.
